The meeting was called to order by Vice Chair Apodaca at 6:00 p.m., in the Norwalk City
Hall, Council Chambers, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Present were
Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Macias, Commissioner Vernola-Salas, and Vice
Chair Apodaca. Chair Lopez joined the meeting at 6:04 p.m. Also present were Alex
Hamilton, Interim Director of Community Development; Austin A. Ching, Deputy City
Attorney; Nancy Lee, Development Services Manager; Kristy Wong, Associate Planner;
Stephanie C. Tapia, Assistant Planner; and Ruth Hoffmann, Administrative Secretary.

MEETING MINUTES

The Planning Commission approved the minutes of the Special Planning Commission
Meeting of February 12, 2025.

As the applicant for Conditional Use Permit No. 2024-02 was running late, the
Commission considered the 2024 Norwalk General Plan and Housing Element Annual
Progress Report first.

THE 2024 NORWALK GENERAL PLAN AND HOUSING ELEMENT ANNUAL
PROGRESS REPORT

Kristy Wong, Associate Planner, presented a report stating that, as required by
Government Code Section 65400(b), every jurisdiction must submit an annual progress
report on the implementation status of the General Plan; that after Planning Commission
review, the item will be scheduled for City Council review and consideration on March 18,
2025; that by April 1st of this year the Progress Report, covering the previous calendar
year, must be submitted to the legislative body of the Department of Housing and
Community Development (HCD) and to the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate
Innovation (LCI).

Ms. Wong stated that the Norwalk General Plan consists of ten (10) Elements consisting
of Land Use, Circulation, Housing, Conservation, Open Space, Noise, Safety, Community
Design, Educational and Cultural Resources, and Utility Infrastructure; that regarding the
Circulation Element for 2024, the City continued construction work to repair/replace
damaged curbs, gutters and sidewalks throughout the City; that the City also continued
design of intersection improvements on Imperial Highway and Bloomfield Avenue;
Studebaker Road and Alondra Boulevard; and that in addition to conducting circulation
improvements, the City also provides public transportation services through the Norwalk
Transit System since 1974.

Next, Ms. Wong commented on the Housing Element. She stated that in February 2023,
the City Council adopted the 2021-2029 Housing Element of the General Plan; that for
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 2
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

the 2024 calendar year, the City issued building permits for 454 residential units; and that
of the 454 building permits,126 units are allocated for affordable housing units.

Associate Planner Wong next commented on the Norwalk Housing Authority (NHA)
indicating that they administer an ongoing Housing Voucher Program; that during 2024,
the NHA assisted an average of 555 families by paying their rent through the Housing
Choice Vouchers, 13 individuals with Mainstream Vouchers, and 32 individuals with
Emergency Housing Vouchers; that in 2023, the City was awarded the Cal-Home Grant
to assist individual first-time homebuyers through deferred-payment loans for down
payment assistance and home rehabilitation; that the program became effective in 2024
to support first-time, low- and moderate-income home buyers in Norwalk to obtain their
first home; that of the six (6) applications, five (5) were approved and one loan was
disbursed to the applicant; and that, in addition to the Home Investment Partnership
(HOME) Program funds were allocated for an affordable housing development of 55 units
in the Norwalk Entertainment District to benefit those at or below eighty percent (80%) of
area median income.

Continuing with her presentation, Ms. Wong shared that regarding Recycling, the City is
committed to “going green”, promoting public awareness on the importance of
recycling/conservation and offering programs for its residents; that these programs
include the Used Oil Block Grants, E-Waste and Shredding events, construction and
demolition recycling, battery recycling program, SHARPS Disposal Program and
mandatory commercial recycling; that during a 2024 event, twenty-seven (27) tons of
electronic waste was diverted from the waste stream along with nine (9) tons of paper
that were shredded and recycled.

Ms. Wong commented on the Open Space Element stating that in 2024, park
improvements included playground installation and amenity improvements at Bob White
Park, New River Park, Vista Verde Park and Holifield Park; that, in addition, the City also
provided athletic field turf renovations at Gerdes Park, Hermosillo Park, Holifield Park,
Lakeside Park, Ramona Park, and Zimmerman Park; that the City also provided annual
landscape maintenance at various City parks.

Regarding the Safety Element, Associate Planner Wong indicated that the programs are,
for the most part, carried out by the Public Safety Department; that the City participates
in the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) which provides programs
educating the public in emergency preparedness; and that, in addition, they continue to
assist the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department to enhance community safety
through crime prevention.

The next item addressed was the Utility Infrastructure Element. Ms. Wong stated that
this Element is intended to ensure that adequate utility levels are provided on both the
sewer system and water system; and that two sewer lift stations have been rehabilitated.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 3
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

Commenting on the Educational and Cultural Resources, Ms. Wong shared that this
Element enhanced the quality of education; that the City continued to work as part of the
Norwalk Education Alliance to help people with higher education, job training and
entrepreneurship within the City; that in 2024 over fifty (50) workshops were held in
collaboration with Los Angeles County agencies, local community college, and local
organizations.

Associate Planner Wong stated that, in conclusion, staff believes that the City has
continued to faithfully implement the City’s General Plan, and recommends that the
Planning Commission approve, by minute motion, a recommendation to the Norwalk City
Council to receive and file the 2024 Norwalk General Plan and Housing Element Annual
Progress Report and direct staff to transmit the report to the Governor’s Office of Land
Use and Climate Innovation (LCI) and the Department of Housing and Community
Development (HCD).

In response to Commissioner Macias’ request for clarification on the qualifications to be
eligible for housing improvements, and who can residents contact, Interim Director of
Community Development Hamilton indicated that for information on any of the City’s
housing programs they can reach out to the City’s Housing staff.

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that the Commission approves this item every year, and she
thanked staff for compiling all the data.

As no other comments were made, it was moved by Commissioner Vernola-Salas and
seconded by Vice Chair Apodaca to approve, by minute motion, a recommendation to the
Norwalk City Council to receive and file the 2024 Norwalk General Plan and Housing
Element Annual Progress Report and direct staff to transmit the report to the Governor’s
Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation (LCI) and the Department of Housing and
Community Development (HCD).

CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 2024-02
Beth Aboulafia of Hinman & Carmichael, LLP for Target Corporation (“Applicant”); a
request to allow the off-site sale of beer, wine and distilled spirits for consumption off the
premises where sold (Type 21 ABC license) and ancillary instructional tasting (Type 86
ABC license) within an existing 135,446 square foot department store (Target). The
subject site is 8.7 acres in size and is generally known as 10600 Firestone Boulevard,
located on the south side of Firestone Boulevard, west of the 605 Freeway (also known
as Assessor’s Parcel Number(s) (“APN”) 8021-003-010; 8021-004-008, 009), in Specific
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 4
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

Plan Area No. 13. Environmental: Consider and find that the proposed project is exempt
from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Section 15301
(Existing Facilities).

Vice Chair Apodaca opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Assistant Planner Tapia
presented a report stating that the request is to permit the off-site sale of beer, wine and
distilled spirits for consumption off the premises where sold (Type 21 ABC license) with
ancillary instructional tasting (Type 86 ABC license) in connection with instructional
tasting events within an existing 135,446 square foot department store (Target) on an 8.7
acres site. Further, she stated that the existing Target store has been selling beer and
wine since 2004 under Conditional Use Permit No. 828 through Planning Commission
Resolution No. 04-18; that Conditional Use Permit No. 828 was modified under Planning
Commission Resolution No. 08-02, which was approved in 2008 and allowed the sale of
containers smaller than 750ml in manufacturers pre-packaged multi-unit quantities; and
that Target’s hours of operation are from 8:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. daily with 40-60
employees per shift.

Further, Ms. Tapia shared that the instructional tasting events will be conducted in a
separate tasting area within the alcoholic beverages display area; that during the
instructional tasting event, the tasting area will be cordoned off by a rope, cable, cord or
other temporary barrier; that no one under 21 will be permitted to enter the designated
tasting area and customers will not be permitted to leave the tasting area with any open
containers of alcoholic beverages; that the Conditions of Approval state that the
instructional tasting events shall only occur on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays between
the hours of 11:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m.; that there are restrictions on quantities and sizes
of alcohol tasting beverage containers for the instructional training; that a video
surveillance system and exterior lighting for the site be provided as well as training and
education of employees regarding alcohol sales. Further, she stated that the request
complies with the Zoning Code and General Plan and is exempt from the California
Environmental Quality Act Guidelines pursuant to Section 15301 (Existing Facilities).

Ms. Tapia stated that to avoid future conflict with the Conditions of Approval, the current
Condition of Approval No. 2 provides that “The Conditions of Approval listed in Planning
Commission Resolution Nos. 04-18 and 08-02 for Conditional Use Permit No. 828 shall
remain in full force and effect. Should any conflict arise between these Conditions of
Approval, the more restrictive requirements shall apply in all cases.” She stated that the
following verbiage should be added at the end of the condition: “with the exception of
Condition No. 17;” that Condition No. 17 indicates that alcohol shall not be sold or offered
for sale, between the hours of 12:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.; that this condition is in conflict
with Condition No. 19 of the 2008 Conditions of Approval which indicate that alcohol shall
not be sold or offered for sale between the hours of 11:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m.; and that
the revised condition accommodates Target’s expanded holiday hours.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 5
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

Further, Ms. Tapia indicated that Condition of Approval No. 30 be revised; that the current
condition states that “The total volume of tastings shall not exceed one fourth of one
ounce per individual per day.” She stated that the revised Condition of Approval No. 30
provides that “Instructional tastings on the subject of wine or distilled spirits are limited to
not more than 3 tastes per person per day. A single tasting of wine shall not exceed 1
oz. and single tasting of distilled spirits shall not exceed ¼ oz. Instructional tastings on
the subject of beer are limited to tastings of not more than 8 oz. per person per day.
Instructional tasting events shall be in strict compliance with all applicable California
Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) regulations.”

Ms. Tapia shared that alcoholic beverage sales will continue to be a very small component
of Target’s overall retail operations; that it is not anticipated to generate detrimental
impacts to the surrounding neighborhood; that, in addition, staff anticipates possible
moderate sales increases; and that staff is recommending that the Planning Commission
adopt Resolution No. 25-01 to approve Conditional Use Permit No. 2024-02 subject to
the revised Condition of Approval Nos. 2 and 30.

Ms. Tapia commented on the Code Requirements letter addressed to the applicant and
attached to the staff report (Attachment D). She stated that condition “m”, which states
that the “Final version to include Public Safety/Code Compliance comments” be deleted.

The applicant’s representative, Beth Aboulafia of Hinman & Carmichael LLP stated that
her flight from Oakland was delayed, and that she very much appreciates the
Commission’s accommodation in switching the agenda order. Further, she stated that
the staff report was very thorough; that Target has been selling beer and wine under an
approved permit at this store for over twenty years; that they are now requesting approval
to upgrade the license type from beer and wine off-sale license to a Type 21 off-site
license that allows beer, wine and distilled spirits to be sold; that this will bring this Target
store in line with more than ninety-five percent (95%) of the Target stores in California
that sell beer, wine and distilled spirits as part of their grocery offerings; that in 2004 when
Target first started licensing alcohol in stores they did not have the grocery component to
their store; that, at that time, they were just applying for beer and wine; that they would
like to be able to offer the full complement of alcoholic beverages as part of the grocery
section; that Target employees will go through a remote Responsible Beverage Server
(RBS) alcohol training approved by ABC, as well as Target’s own in-house training
program; that with respect to the instructional tasting license, this allows suppliers to come
into the store on an occasional basis for tasting of a particular product for customers in
the store; that as indicated in the staff report, those tastings have to be conducted under
very strict ABC guidelines with respect to the area being cordoned off, and that no alcohol
will be taken out of the area; and that, as shown on the slides, the tasting area is very
small.

In response to Vice-Chair Apodaca’s request for clarification if they promote the tasting
events ahead of time, Ms. Aboulafia stated that there could be advertising if a particular
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 6
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

wine maker is scheduled to hold a tasting event at a certain time. She stated that Target
has not started this program yet which, she believes, will start some time during the middle
of the year; that there are about a dozen Target stores that have added the Type 86
licenses so that Target can start implementing these tastings, and that there are about
two dozen that are in the application process.

Commissioner Vernola-Salas commented on the hours of the tasting events, and she
asked if they would be holding the event for the full eight hours. Ms. Aboulafia indicated
that the tasting events would probably be conducted for a couple of hours, most likely
between Friday and Sunday during certain time periods.

In response to Commissioner Vernola-Salas’ question how are they going to make sure
that youths will not be served, Ms. Aboulafia stated that the tasting area will probably not
be more than fifty (50) square feet; that it most likely will be located at the end of an aisle
and cordoned off; and that they believe that no more than one or two people would be at
the event at the same time.

Commissioner Vernola-Salas asked how would they know if a person has had two or
three tastes. Ms. Aboulafia replied that the tasting is only taking place for a couple of
hours by one server in a small area; that it will be monitored; and that the servers will
have responsible beverage service training.

Mr. Jack Cornejo stated that he is in opposition to the request; that he received
clarification that the request is for changing the permit by adding distilled spirits to the
beer and wine sales; that after listening to the presentation and to the comments made
by the applicant, the issue is the instructional tasting to which he is strongly opposed at
the Target store; that some of the Commissioners asked for clarification about the
enforcement of conditions, which he appreciated; that he has concerns whether the area
will be fully monitored and persons will not be able to get multiple tastings; and how would
they deal with a person who comes into the store inebriated and goes to all the eligible
tastings.

Vice Chair Apodaca asked the applicant if she wishes to make a rebuttal statement.

Ms. Aboulafia stated that the instructional tasting license carries with it the same
obligations that traditional on-sale and off-sale licenses carry; that it is prohibited to serve
or sell alcohol to anyone who appears intoxicated; and that the employees and the
suppliers who conduct the tastings will be vigilant. Further, she stated that, for
clarification, there are limits on the number of tastes and volume of taste that differ for
each type of alcoholic beverage; and that she wants to make it clear that only one type of
alcoholic beverage can be served at any given tasting.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Vice Chair Apodaca
closed the public hearing.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 7
Minutes of the Special Meeting  February 26, 2025

Commissioner Barragan indicated that she has read all of the conditions of approval, and
that she has no issues with granting this permit.

Commissioner Macias and Commissioner Vernola-Salas both stated that all of their
questions have been answered.

In response to Chair Lopez’ inquiry as to number of ounces per tasting, Vice Chair
Apodaca replied that revised Condition No. 30 states that wine shall not exceed 1 oz.,
distilled spirits shall not exceed ¼ oz. and beer shall not exceed 8 oz. per person per day.

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that instructional tasting is a new concept at Target; that she
sees no issues with the small area proposed for the tasting; that the tasting event will be
monitored; that the employees will be trained; and that Target is a responsible
corporation.

It was moved by Commissioner Vernola-Salas and seconded by Vice Chair Apodaca to:
a) Adopt Resolution No. 25-01 to approve Conditional Use Permit (CUP) No. 2024-02
subject to the revised Conditions of Approval No. 30 which state that “Instructional
tastings on the subject of wine or distilled spirits are limited to not more than 3 tastes per
person per day. A single tasting of wine shall not exceed 1 oz. and single tasting of
distilled spirits shall not exceed ¼ oz. Instructional tastings on the subject of beer are
limited to tastings of not more than 8 oz. per person per day. Instructional tasting events
shall be in strict compliance with all applicable California Department of Alcoholic
Beverage Control (ABC) regulations;” (b) That Condition of Approval No. 2 refers to
Resolution Nos. 04-18 and 08-02 for CUP 828; that the language states that “The
Conditions of Approval listed in these two resolutions shall remain in full force and effect;
that should any conflict arise between these conditions, the more restrictive requirements
shall apply in all cases;” that language be added at the end of the condition that states
“with the exception of Condition No. 17”; (that this condition indicates that alcohol shall
not be sold or offered for sale between the hours of 12:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.); and c)
Consider and find that the proposed project is exempt from CEQA pursuant to Section
15301 (Existing Facilities).

Project Description:

The Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan (“Specific Plan”) allows a mixed-use development
with up to 66,647 square feet of neighborhood commercial uses, 13,500 square feet of active
commercial uses, a hotel with up to 150 rooms, 770 residential units (40% of the units will be
designated as “affordable,”) and 3.7 acres of open space/parkland uses on a 32.3 acre property
located at 13200 Bloomfield Avenue (“Subject Site”).

A copy of the Specific Plan can be found in the following link:

Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan

Background:

On July 10, 2024, the Planning Commission held a public hearing for review and consideration
of the Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan and recommended with a 5-0 vote that the City

Council approve the Specific Plan.

On November 19, 2024, City Council completed the public hearing for review of the Specific
Plan and as a First Reading, adopted the Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan and adopted
Resolution No. 24-58 certifying the project Final Environmental Impact Report (FEIR SCH No.
2022070103) with a 5-0 vote. On January 21, 2025, City Council, as a Second Reading,
adopted Ordinance No. 24-1754 establishing Specific Plan Area No. 17, the “Norwalk Transit
Village Specific Plan” which became effective on February 21, 2025.

On November 25, 2024, the Planning Commission adopted PC Resolution No. 24-12 finding
that the disposition of the Property is in conformance with the City’s General Plan pursuant to
Government Code Section 65402.

On December 3, 2024, City Council adopted Resolution No. 24-61 approving the Purchase
and Sales Agreement (“PSA”) by and between the State of California and the City for the
Subject Site.

On December 3, 2024, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 24-62 declaring the Southern
California Youth Correctional Reception Center and Clinic (“CYA”) located at 13200 Bloomfield
Avenue exempt surplus land pursuant to Government Code Sections 54221(F)(1) and adopted
an ordinance approving a Disposition and Development Agreement (DDA), by and between
the City of Norwalk (“City”) and Lewis Land Developers, LLC (“Developer”).

Request:

The Developer is requesting approval of Development Agreement (DA) No. 2025-0001 to
expressly define a development project’s rules, regulations, commitments, and policies for a
specific period of time for the development of the Specific Plan area. Development
Agreements such as this are commonly known as “Statutory Development Agreements”
(SDA). The purpose of an SDA is to “lock in” entitlement approvals to provide for more certainty
in the entitlement process.

Authority:

The Development Agreement Act (California Government Code §65864 et seq.) authorizes
cities to enter into binding development agreements with persons having a legal or equitable
interest in real property for the development of such property, all for the purposes of
strengthening the public planning process, encouraging private participation and
comprehensive planning and identifying the economic costs of such development.

Analysis:

Summary of Key Terms of DA No. 2025-0001:
  • Term: Ten (10) years from the Effective Date of this Agreement (the “Term”), with an
  automatic additional five (5) years if certificates of occupancy have been issued for at
  least 150 total Residential Units by the expiration of the initial Term.

  •  Subdivision Maps. Any tentative subdivision map or tentative parcel map approved for
  the property after the Effective Date shall automatically be extended for the term of the
  agreement as provided under the provisions of Government Code section 66452.6(a).
  •  Assignment. Developer has the right to assign the Agreement in whole or in part to
  any person, partnership, limited liability company, corporation or other legal entity at any
  time during the term of this Agreement that acquires a fee or ground leasehold interest
  in any of the Property (a “Transfer”), subject to approval by the City. This is important to

  this magnitude. This provision does not apply to restrict or limit any assignment of this
  Agreement to an Affordable Housing Builder as part of the Transfer of the Affordable
  Parcel to the City or the Affordable Housing Builder.
  •  Vested Development Rights. Developer acquires vested right to develop the Project on
  the Property in accordance with, and to the extent of, the Development Approvals that
  are in place at the time the Development Agreement is entered into by the parties during
  the Term of the Development Agreement.
  •  Public Benefits:
  o Public Park. In lieu of the payment of any Quimby park fees or other Development
  Impact Fees for parks or open space, Developer will construct and dedicate two
  (2) public parks within the Specific Plan area.
  o Affordable Housing. The development of 200 affordable housing will contribute
  to the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RNHA) requirement.
  o Art in Public Places. Developer may elect to install art work or pay an in-lieu fee
  equal to one percent of the total project cost.

Environmental Assessment:

The California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) and the CEQA Guidelines allow the City to
rely on the previously certified Norwalk Transit Village Specific Plan FEIR unless a subsequent
or supplement Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”) is required. None of the conditions
requiring a subsequent or supplemental EIR under CEQA Guidelines Sections 15162 and
15163 have occurred. Accordingly, taking into consideration the analysis in the FEIR, DA No.
202502 is within the envelope of the FEIR prepared for the Norwalk Transit Village Specific
Plan area and no further environmental review is required.

Further, adoption of the proposed resolution is exempt from the CEQA pursuant to the
“Common Sense” exemption set forth under Section 15061(b)(3), which provides that CEQA
applies only to projects which have the potential for causing a significant effect on the
environment and also states that where it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility
that DA No. 2025-0001 may have a significant effect on the environment.
